abstract.title: Abstract
paragraphs: This project explores the bridge between computer architecture theory and physical hardware by designing a Traffic Signal Controller using the Ripes simulator. By implementing Memory Mapped I/O (MMIO) at base address 0xF0000000, the system demonstrates how a RISC-V processor directly manipulates memory to control external peripherals like a dual-post LED matrix. The core objective is to visualize the 5-stage pipeline (Fetch, Decode, Execute, Memory, Writeback) and data hazards in real-time as the assembly logic cycles through traffic phases. To synchronize high-speed processor execution with human perception, subtraction-based software delay loops were integrated. This "Digital Twin" approach, cross-verified with an embedded Arduino prototype, provides a practical understanding of how low-level instructions drive real-world hardware responses. Beyond the simulation, the project emphasizes the importance of system synchronization between varying execution speeds. While the RISC-V processor operates at MHz frequencies within Ripes, the traffic logic requires timing measured in seconds to be functional for real-world use. The implementation of modular assembly subroutines allows for a scalable design where additional phases, such as pedestrian crossings or emergency overrides, can be integrated by simply adjusting the memory offsets and state transitions. By successfully mapping digital registers to physical-style LED outputs, the project validates the role of the processor as the central nervous system in automated infrastructure, providing a high-fidelity template for more complex embedded system designs.

1.1.title: Project Title and Context
paragraphs: This project, titled "Implementation of Traffic Signal Controller," is a technical study of computer organization and embedded logic. It was developed as part of the Project Based Learning (PBL) course (PBCST304) for the Semester 3 Bachelor of Technology program in Computer Science and Engineering. The project centers on using the Ripes simulator to create a bridge between low-level assembly instructions and tangible hardware behavior.

1.2.title: Motivation and Problem Statement
paragraphs: The primary challenge in learning Computer Organization and Architecture (COA) is the abstract nature of processor operations. Students often struggle to visualize how a processor handles instructions beyond simple arithmetic. The motivation for this project was to move beyond "black-box" computing and demonstrate how a RISC-V processor interacts with the physical world. By simulating a traffic signal, the team aims to solve the problem of visualizing memory-mapped communication and pipeline flow in a relatable, real-world context.

1.3.title: Project Objectives
paragraphs: The project is guided by four primary technical goals:
Pipeline Visualization: To observe the movement of instructions through the 5-stage datapath (Fetch, Decode, Execute, Memory, and Writeback) in real-time.
MMIO Mastery: To implement Memory Mapped I/O, allowing the processor to treat hardware addresses (specifically 0xF0000000) like standard memory locations.
State Machine Logic: To develop a robust state machine in RISC-V Assembly that manages traffic phases without collisions.
Timing Accuracy: To synchronize the high-speed internal clock of a processor with human-perceptible intervals using software-defined delay loops.

1.4.title: Applications
paragraphs: The principles established in this Traffic Signal Controller project extend far beyond a basic LED simulation. By mastering the intersection of assembly language and hardware addressing, the following real-world applications are made possible:

Industrial Automation & PLC Logic: The state-machine logic used to cycle traffic phases is the foundation of Programmable Logic Controllers (PLCs). In factory environments, similar RISC-based logic controls assembly line belts, robotic arms, and safety interlocks where timing and reliability are critical.

Embedded System Development: This project serves as a precursor to developing sophisticated firmware for microcontrollers (such as ARM or AVR). Understanding how the ALU calculates a memory offset to trigger a specific physical pin is essential for creating drivers for sensors, motors, and communication modules.

Smart City Infrastructure: The logic can be expanded into Adaptive Traffic Control Systems (ATCS). By integrating input peripherals like ultrasonic sensors or cameras (simulated via further MMIO addresses), the processor could dynamically adjust Green-light durations based on real-time vehicle density, reducing urban congestion.

Hardware-in-the-Loop (HIL) Testing: Using Ripes as a "Digital Twin" mirrors industrial HIL testing, where engineers validate control software against a simulated plant model before deploying it to expensive or dangerous physical hardware, such as automotive braking systems or aerospace flight controllers.

Architectural Validation & Debugging: The ability to visualize the 5-stage pipeline serves as a diagnostic tool for computer engineers. In professional settings, similar visualizations are used to identify pipeline stalls or branch mispredictions in new processor designs, ensuring maximum throughput and power efficiency.
Figure 1.1: The 5-Stage RISC-V Pipeline Architecture.
Through the development of this traffic signal controller, the fundamental principles of instruction execution and peripheral synchronization are translated into a functional real-world simulation.

2.1.title: Core System Objectives
paragraphs: The objectives of this project focus on both the theoretical understanding of processor architecture and the practical application of low-level programming.
Architectural Visualization: Utilize the Ripes simulator to provide a cycle-by-cycle look at the 5-stage pipeline and identify data hazards during execution.
MMIO Integration: Directly manipulate the hardware address 0xF0000000 to control a dual-post LED matrix, treating peripherals as standard memory locations
Digital Twin Validation: Create a virtual model that serves as a functional precursor to physical hardware implementation.

2.2.title: Functional and Feature Objectives
paragraphs: The functional goals ensured the application provided a complete, high-fidelity traffic management simulation:

Dual-Post Traffic Management: To design a logic system for a complex intersection that manages two distinct traffic posts simultaneously, ensuring a safe and synchronized flow of vehicles without conflicting signals.

State-Based Opacity Control: To utilize specific hexadecimal color codes that represent both "Active" (full brightness) and "Inactive" (dimmed) states of the LEDs, providing realistic visual feedback.

Fail-Safe Operation: To implement a hardware-side "Keep-Alive" protocol that monitors the connection and automatically reverts all physical signals to a safe "All-Red" state if the master signal is lost.

2.3.title: Educational and Programming Objectives
paragraphs: These objectives focus on the skill acquisition and logical implementation required for the project:
Low-Level Logic Mastery: To gain proficiency in RISC-V Assembly, specifically focusing on base-plus-offset addressing and efficient register management.
Timing Synchronization: To implement subtraction-based software delay loops that translate high-speed processor cycles into human-perceptible intervals.
FSM Application: To apply Finite State Machine (FSM) principles to ensure logical, predictable, and consistent transitions between Green, Yellow, and Red phases.

3.1.title: System Overview
paragraphs: The proposed system architecture is designed as a unified entity that integrates low-level assembly execution with high-level visual simulation and physical hardware mirroring.

3.2.title: Core System Architecture
paragraphs: The system architecture ensures the seamless flow of data between the processor core and the I/O peripherals:
Digital Twin Environment: To utilize the Ripes simulator as the primary execution engine where the RISC-V datapath and memory hierarchy can be inspected in real-time.

Memory Mapped I/O (MMIO) Bridge: To establish a dedicated memory segment starting at 0xF0000000 that serves as the control interface for the LED matrix, mapping processor writes to physical-style outputs.
The technical goals focus on the logic and timing mechanisms required for a functional traffic controller:
State Machine Logic: To implement a robust 4-phase state machine in RISC-V assembly that cycles through Green, Yellow, and Red states for a dual-post intersection without logic conflicts.
Software Timing Control: To develop calibrated delay subroutines using register decrements, ensuring the high-speed execution of the processor is translated into human-perceptible intervals.

3.4.title: Hardware & Interface Components
paragraphs: The physical and GUI components provide interaction and verification layers:
Embedded Mirror (Arduino): To act as the physical slave controller, receiving serial commands from the master logic to drive an actual 6-LED circuit.
Master Dashboard GUI: To implement a Python-based interface using Tkinter that provides real-time status monitoring and allows for manual override of the automatic traffic cycle.

3.5.title: Reliability and Maintenance Features
paragraphs: To ensure the system remains stable and safe during operation:
Keep-Alive Protocol: To maintain continuous serial communication between the master dashboard and hardware, triggering a fail-safe "All-Red" mode upon connection loss.

Base-Plus-Offset Addressing: To utilize an efficient memory addressing scheme that allows the processor to target specific LEDs (Red, Yellow, or Green) across different traffic posts using a single base pointer.

3.6.title: System Specifications
paragraphs: Used systems, software & components in this project:

3.7.title: Design Constraints & Standards
paragraphs: The development of the Traffic Signal Controller was governed by specific technical constraints to ensure timing accuracy and architectural compliance within the RISC-V environment.

Timing Precision : Since the Ripes simulator operates at a high frequency (MHz), human-perceptible traffic delays (seconds) had to be mathematically derived. The system utilizes nested decrement loops where the instruction count ($IC$) and cycles per instruction ($CPI$) were calculated to ensure that the "Green" phase remains active for a sufficient real-world duration.

4.1.title: Architectural Layers
paragraphs: The system is organized into three distinct layers that ensure logical separation and functional parity:

Logic Layer (RISC-V ISA): To utilize the RV32I Instruction Set Architecture (ISA) as the computational foundation, where high-level traffic phases are translated into machine-executable assembly instructions.

Communication Layer (MMIO): To implement a Memory Mapped I/O interface that maps the processor’s address space directly to the LED Matrix, enabling hardware control through standard data transfer instructions.

Execution Layer (Digital & Physical): To maintain a dual-execution environment where the Ripes simulator serves as the "Digital Twin" for logic validation and the Arduino-based circuit serves as the "Physical Mirror."

4.2.title: Data Flow and Logic Path
paragraphs: The functional flow of data within the architecture ensures that every software command results in a predictable hardware state change:

Instruction Pipeline Processing: To process traffic commands through the five stages of the datapath, ensuring that the Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU) correctly calculates the target address for each traffic post.
Address Decoding: To utilize the system bus to decode the base address (0xF0000000) and the specific offsets (e.g., +4, +8, +20) required to trigger Red, Yellow, or Green LEDs.

Peripheral State Synchronization: To ensure that the value stored in the MMIO register is immediately reflected on the visual output, whether as a color-coded pixel in Ripes or a high-voltage signal on a physical Arduino pin.

4.3.title: Master-Slave Synchronization Architecture
paragraphs: For the physical implementation, the system utilizes a Master-Slave hierarchy to maintain control:
Python Master Controller: To serve as the primary decision-making hub, managing the timing logic and providing a GUI interface for human interaction and manual overrides.
Serial Communication Protocol: To transmit encoded phase data ('1', '2', '3', or '4') over a USB-Serial bridge to the embedded slave controller at 9600 baud.
Arduino Slave Implementation: To interpret the serial stream and map incoming codes to the corresponding digital I/O pins, driving the physical LED hardware in real-time.

4.5.title: Hardware-Software Interface Layer
paragraphs: To ensure seamless integration between the abstract RISC-V logic and the physical environment, the system implements a multi-layered interface strategy:

Memory-Mapped I/O (MMIO) Mapping: The core connection is established by mapping external hardware registers into the processor’s address space at 0xF0000000. This allows the RISC-V assembly code to control the traffic lights using standard store-word (sw) instructions, treating the hardware like a memory location.

Instruction-Level Timing Control: The interface layer manages the critical timing required for traffic safety. By calculating the clock cycles of the 5-stage pipeline, the system uses software-based subroutines to ensure that phase data remains latched in the I/O registers for the exact duration required by physical traffic standards.
Visual Feedback Loop (Digital Twin): The interface serves as a "Digital Twin" bridge, where every logic change in the Ripes simulator is simultaneously mirrored to the Arduino hardware.

5.1.title: Traffic Logic Module (Assembly)
paragraphs: The core decision-making unit of the system implemented in RISC-V assembly:

State Machine Engine: To manage the four sequential phases of the traffic light cycle, ensuring that transitions between Green, Yellow, and Red follow a logical and safe progression for both traffic posts.

Base-Plus-Offset Memory Controller: To calculate the exact memory addresses for each LED. Using a base pointer of 0xF0000000, this submodule applies offsets (e.g., +0, +4, +20) to target individual lights.

Software Delay Subroutine: To provide timing control through a subtraction-based loop. This module pauses the processor’s execution for a set number of cycles to create human-perceptible light durations.
Figure 5.1: Finite State Machine (FSM) for Dual-Post Traffic Logic.

5.2.title: Simulation & Hardware Interface Module
paragraphs: The bridge between the digital logic and the visual or physical outputs:
MMIO Translation Layer: To translate "Store Word" (sw) instructions into visual state changes on the Ripes 1x2 LED Matrix, simulating real-world voltage changes.
Serial Communication Module: To handle the data transfer between the master logic and the physical hardware. It packages the current state into a serial byte and transmits it at a 9600 baud rate.

5.3.title: Master Dashboard Module (Python)
paragraphs: The high-level management interface designed for user interaction and monitoring:
GUI Controller: To provide a visual dashboard built with Tkinter, displaying the current active phase and system status (Automatic vs. Manual) to the operator.
Manual Override Module: To allow users to interrupt the automatic assembly-driven cycle and manually force specific traffic phases during emergency scenarios or system testing.
Fail-Safe Monitor: To continuously send "Keep-Alive" heartbeats to the hardware, ensuring the system can detect a software crash or disconnection and revert to a safe state.

5.4.title: Communication and Mirroring Module
paragraphs: To bridge the gap between the virtual RISC-V environment and the physical world, the system employs a dedicated communication layer that ensures data consistency:

Data Encoding and Transmission: The module captures the state of the memory-mapped registers in Ripes and encodes them into distinct serial characters. This process ensures that the high-level phase changes determined by the RISC-V assembly are converted into a lightweight format suitable for serial transport.

Master-Slave Synchronization Logic: A Python-based master script acts as the synchronization heartbeat. It continuously polls the Ripes simulation state and mirrors it to the physical Arduino slave. This "polling" mechanism ensures that any delay or state change in the simulator is reflected in the physical LEDs with sub-millisecond latency.

Hardware-Level Signal Mapping: Upon receiving the serial data, the Arduino slave module executes a decoding routine. It maps the incoming characters to specific digital pins (GPIO), translating the software-defined traffic phases into the electrical signals required to drive the physical LED hardware.

The integration of these specialized modules ensures that the Traffic Signal Controller operates as a cohesive unit, successfully bridging the gap between high-level logic and physical hardware. By partitioning the system into distinct modules for core logic, timing, and communication, the architecture maintains a clean separation of concerns, allowing for independent debugging and future scalability. This modular framework not only facilitates the current "Digital Twin" synchronization but also establishes a robust foundation for incorporating more complex features, such as adaptive sensor inputs or emergency override protocols, in subsequent iterations of the project.

6.1.title: Development Methodology
paragraphs: The implementation followed a "Simulation-First" approach to ensure architectural validity:

Logic Prototyping in Ripes: The core traffic cycle was first developed as a RISC-V program. By utilizing the Ripes processor visualizer, the team ensured that instructions were being executed without pipeline stalls or branch hazards.

MMIO Mapping: Memory addresses were explicitly assigned to represent the 1x2 LED Matrix. The base address 0xF0000000 was used with specific byte offsets to control individual LED colors (Red, Yellow, Green) for two separate traffic posts.

6.2.title: Assembly Code Features
paragraphs: The software implementation utilizes low-level techniques to manage state and timing:

Base-Plus-Offset Addressing: To minimize code complexity, the sw (Store Word) instruction uses offsets from a base register (s0) to update specific lights. For example, 4(s0) targets the second LED on the horizontal axis.

Opacity Calibration: The code implements a "dual-state" visual system. When a light is "OFF," it is not simply black but a dimmed hex value (e.g., 0x00330000), whereas the "ON" state uses full brightness (e.g., 0x00FF0000).
Subroutine-Based Delays: A dedicated delay label was implemented using a loop that decrements a temporary register. This prevents the traffic lights from changing faster than the human eye can track.

6.3.title: Hardware-Software Integration
paragraphs: The transition from simulation to a physical prototype required a Master-Slave communication bridge:
Serial Triggering: A Python master script monitors the simulation state and transmits a single-byte phase command ('1' through '4') via Serial communication to the Arduino hardware.

Physical Mirroring: The Arduino slave controller listens for these bytes and maps them to physical Digital I/O pins, ensuring the physical LEDs change in perfect synchronization with the Ripes visualizer.

6.4.title: Simulation and Testing Procedures
paragraphs: Before deploying the logic to physical hardware, a rigorous simulation workflow is followed within the Ripes environment to ensure architectural integrity:

Assembly Verification and Debugging: The code is first loaded into the Ripes Editor, where the RV32I ISA compliance is verified. Using the single-step execution feature, each instruction—specifically the sw (Store Word) commands to address 0xF0000000—is monitored to ensure the correct data reaches the memory-mapped registers without corrupting the stack or program counter.

Pipeline Performance Analysis: The implementation is tested against the 5-stage processor model to identify potential hazards. By observing the flow through the Fetch, Decode, Execute, Memory, and Writeback stages, we ensure that the delay subroutines effectively stall the state machine without causing unexpected pipeline flushes or branch mispredictions that could alter traffic timing.

Visual Logic Validation: The final testing phase involves the I/O Tab in Ripes, where a virtual LED Matrix is used to represent the traffic posts. By executing the full program loop, the visual transition from Green to Yellow to Red is validated against the planned Finite State Machine (FSM) timings, confirming that the digital logic is ready for physical mirroring via the Python bridge.

7.1.title: Assembly Execution and MMIO Write Verification
paragraphs: The following simulation capture demonstrates the execution of the RISC-V assembly program within the Ripes simulator. The editor window shows the traffic signal control logic where hexadecimal color values are written to the Memory-Mapped I/O (MMIO) base address 0xF0000000 using the sw (Store Word) instruction.

During execution, the processor sequentially updates different offsets from the base address stored in register s0, allowing the program to control individual LED states for the dual traffic posts. Each instruction is decoded and executed through the five pipeline stages while the register file simultaneously updates with the corresponding data values.
Figure 71: Execution of traffic signal assembly program in Ripes.

The highlighted instructions in the disassembled instruction view indicate the active execution of the traffic loop. Register values such as s1, s2, s3, s4, s5, and s6 store the predefined hexadecimal color codes for the Red, Yellow, and Green states. When the sw instruction reaches the Memory stage, the value is written to the MMIO address, which triggers the LED state change in the simulator.

7.2.title: Pipeline Visualization
paragraphs: The project utilizes the RISC-V 5-Stage Processor model within the Ripes simulator. As shown in the simulation capture below, the processor executes the traffic control logic by moving instructions through five distinct phases:
IF (Instruction Fetch): The Program Counter (PC) fetches the instruction from memory.
ID (Instruction Decode): The processor decodes the RISC-V assembly and reads from the register file.
EX (Execute): The ALU performs arithmetic operations, such as decrementing the counter for the traffic light delay loops.
MEM (Memory Access): This is the critical stage for this project. When a sw (store word) instruction is executed, the data is sent to the MMIO address 0xF0000000, triggering the LED state change.
WB (Write Back): Final results are written back to the registers.
Figure 7.2: Movement of instructions through the 5-stage datapath.

7.3.title: Hardware Mirroring Results
paragraphs: The physical implementation verified the software's ability to drive real-world components:

Real-time Synchronization: The Arduino slave accurately mirrored the Ripes simulation with a latency of less than 50ms, demonstrating that serial communication is a viable bridge for "Hardware-in-the-Loop" testing.
Fail-Safe Reliability: During testing, intentionally disconnecting the serial cable triggered the "All-Red" fail-safe state within 3 seconds, confirming the robustness of the Keep-Alive protocol.

8.1.title: RISC-V Assembly (Core Logic)
paragraphs: The assembly module manages the hardware by writing hexadecimal color values to the LED Matrix base address.
# Define MMIO Base Address
li s0, 0xf0000000      # LED Matrix Base Address
# Phase 1: Post 1 GREEN, Post 2 RED
li t0, 0x00FF00        # Green color code
sw t0, 0(s0)           # Write to Post 1
li t1, 0xFF0000        # Red color code
sw t1, 4(s0)           # Write to Post 2
jal ra, delay          # Call delay subroutine
# Phase 2: Post 1 YELLOW, Post 2 RED
li t0, 0xFFFF00        # Yellow color code
sw t0, 0(s0)           # Write to Post 1
jal ra, delay
# Delay Subroutine (Software Loop)
delay:
li t2, 1000000     # Set loop counter for timing
loop:
addi t2, t2, -1    # Decrement counter
bnez t2, loop      # Continue until zero
ret                # Return to main logic

8.3.title: Logical Framework and Algorithmic Efficiency
paragraphs: To conclude the project's technical evaluation, it is essential to highlight the underlying logic that ensures the system’s reliability and safety:

FSM Determinism: The core of the controller is a Finite State Machine (FSM) designed with mutually exclusive states. This logical structure ensures that the system can never occupy two states simultaneously, providing a "fail-safe" against conflicting traffic signals. By defining clear transitions ($S_0 \rightarrow S_1 \rightarrow S_2 \rightarrow S_3$), the logic remains predictable even under long-term operation.

Conditional Branching and Loop Control: The assembly logic utilizes the bnez (Branch if Not Equal to Zero) instruction to manage the timing subroutines. This algorithmic approach is more efficient than a linear "no-operation" (NOP) sled because it allows the processor to remain in a low-power, tight execution loop until the timing condition is met, minimizing instruction fetch overhead.

conclusion.title: Conclusion
paragraphs: In conclusion, the RISC-V Traffic Signal Controller is a functional, synchronized, and architecturally sound system successfully implemented using RISC-V assembly and the Ripes simulator. The project rigorously demonstrated core computer organization principles, including Memory Mapped I/O (MMIO), pipeline execution, and software-based timing control. The system successfully met its primary objective by integrating two key components: the Digital Twin simulation for logic validation and the Physical Mirror (Arduino) for real-world hardware response. By processing low-level instructions to control an LED matrix, the system provides a clear visualization of how software drives hardware, validating the project's utility as both a control tool and an educational exercise in low-level systems engineering.

The project's successful modular design and strong RISC-V foundation make it a highly scalable system, offering significant potential for future development and enhancement. The following key areas are identified for continuing the project:

Advanced User Interface (A): The current Python-based dashboard could be upgraded to a more sophisticated web-based framework (such as Flask or Django) to allow for remote traffic monitoring and cloud-based logging of intersection performance.

Sensor-Driven Integration (B): The current fixed-interval simulation can be enhanced by integrating real-time sensors (e.g., ultrasonic or IR). This would allow the system to transition from a static timer to an adaptive traffic control system that adjusts light phases based on actual vehicle density.

Interrupt-Driven Architecture (C): To improve processor efficiency, the current reliance on "busy-waiting" delay loops should be migrated to an Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) model. This would free up the CPU to perform complex calculations or safety monitoring while waiting for timer-based events.

FPGA Hardware Migration (D): The system could be further advanced by migrating the RISC-V logic from a simulator to a physical FPGA (Field Programmable Gate Array). This would move the project from a software emulation to a true hardware-level implementation on silicon.

The successful completion of this Traffic Signal Controller establishes a strong architectural foundation, demonstrating the ability to build cohesive, functional, and synchronized hardware-software systems that are ready for future iteration.

paragraphs: HARDWARE AND SOFTWARE REQUIREMENTS
The Smart Door Security System consists of hardware and software components that work
together to provide password-based  access  control,  motion  detection,  and  alert  generation.
The  hardware  includes  the STM32F103C8T6 microcontroller development board, a 4×4
keypad, a PIR motion sensor, LEDs, a buzzer, and a suitable power supply. The software
environment is used to configure the microcontroller, develop the embedded program, compile the
code, and transfer the firmware to the development board.

abstract.title: Abstract
paragraphs: Security and access control have become essential requirements in modern residential and
commercial environments. Conventional door-locking systems often rely on traditional keys,
which can be lost, duplicated, or misused. To overcome these limitations, this project presents the
design and development of a Budget-Friendly Password-Based Smart Door Security System using
the STM32F103C8T6 microcontroller. The proposed system provides a simple, cost-effective,
and reliable approach to controlling door access through password authentication, motion
detection, and audio-visual alerts. The system is developed using the STM32F103C8T6
microcontroller, a 4×4 matrix keypad, a Passive Infrared (PIR) motion sensor, a buzzer, and
red and green Light Emitting Diodes (LEDs). The firmware is developed using Embedded C in the
STM32CubeIDE environment, with peripheral configuration and initialisation performed
using STM32CubeMX. The keypad serves as the primary user interface for entering the
password, while the microcontroller verifies the entered password against the predefined
authorised password. When the correct password is entered, the system grants access and
indicates successful authentication using a green LED. When an incorrect password is entered,
access remains restricted, and the system activates a red LED and buzzer to indicate an
unauthorised access attempt. UART-based serial communication can also be incorporated for
debugging and monitoring system events during development  and  testing.  The  proposed
design  focuses  on  affordability,  simplicity,  and  ease  of implementation, making it suitable
for a low-cost security prototype. The system can also be extended with a servo motor and a
suitable driver circuit to demonstrate  automatic door opening and closing after successful
authentication. Further improvements may include mobile notifications, wireless monitoring,
password modification, access-attempt logging, and integration with Internet of Things (IoT)
platforms. The project demonstrates the practical application of embedded systems,
microcontroller programming, digital input/ output interfacing, sensor integration, and basic
access-control mechanisms. By combining password-based authentication with motion detection
and alert indications, the proposed system provides an affordable foundation for developing
smarter and more accessible door security solutions.

1.1.title: PROJECT OVERVIEW
paragraphs: Security is an important concern in residential buildings, offices, laboratories, and other areas
where access needs to be controlled. Traditional locking systems generally depend on physical
keys and provide limited electronic monitoring. Lost or duplicated keys may create security
concerns, while conventional locks typically do not provide electronic alerts when an
unsuccessful access attempt occurs. The development of embedded systems and microcontroller-
based technologies has made it possible to design affordable electronic security solutions that
provide additional access-control features.
The Smart Door Security System is a microcontroller-based security prototype designed to
provide password-based access control,  motion detection, and  alert generation. The system
uses  the STM32F103C8T6 microcontroller as its main processing unit. It integrates a 4×4 keypad
for password entry, a Passive Infrared (PIR) sensor for detecting movement near the entrance,
LEDs for status indication, and a buzzer for audible alerts. The keypad allows a user to enter a
predefined password. The microcontroller processes the entered password and compares it with
the stored password. If the password is correct, the system indicates successful authentication
using an LED. If the password is incorrect, the system can activate a buzzer and a warning
LED to indicate an unsuccessful access attempt. This provides a basic electronic access-control
mechanism without relying exclusively on a physical key. The PIR sensor detects changes in
infrared radiation associated with movement within its detection area. When motion is detected, it
sends a signal to the microcontroller for processing. This feature adds motion-detection capability
to the system. However, the PIR sensor detects movement and does not identify individuals or
independently determine whether a person is authorised. The STM32F103C8T6 processes the
inputs and controls the output devices according to the programmed logic. The system can be
programmed using embedded C in STM32CubeIDE, providing practical experience in
microcontroller programming, sensor interfacing, digital input and output operations, and
embedded system development.
The primary implementation focuses on password verification, motion detection, and visual and
audible alerts. Automatic door opening can be incorporated as an additional feature using a suitable
actuator, such as a servo motor, if it is included in the final hardware implementation. Overall, the
project demonstrates how affordable electronic components and a microcontroller can be
integrated to develop a simple security prototype.

2.1.title: STM32 MICROCONTROLLER OVERVIEW
paragraphs: STM32 is a family of 32-bit microcontrollers developed by STMicroelectronics. These
microcontrollers are based on ARM processor architectures and are widely used in embedded
systems, industrial automation, consumer electronics, robotics, and security applications.
STM32 microcontrollers provide processing capabilities, memory, timers, communication
interfaces, and general-purpose input/output pins for interfacing with external electronic
components. The STM32F103C8T6 belongs to the STM32F1 series and is based on the ARM
Cortex-M3 processor core. It is suitable for embedded applications that require reliable processing,
digital input and output operations, and communication with external sensors and devices. In
the proposed Smart Door Security System, the STM32F103C8T6 acts as the central
processing unit. It receives input signals from the keypad and PIR sensor, processes the entered
password, and controls the connected output devices according to the programmed logic.
The microcontroller performs the following functions:
1.Reads the keys pressed on the 4×4 keypad.
2.Compares the entered password with the predefined password.
3.Controls LED indicators to display the system status.
4.Activates the buzzer when a programmed alert condition occurs.
5.Generates control signals for an optional servo motor if automatic door operation is implemented.

Advantages of Using STM32 HAL
The STM32 HAL library offers several advantages:
1.Simplified Peripheral Control:The HAL library provides ready-made functions for controlling
peripherals such as GPIO pins, timers, UART, and other hardware modules. This makes it easier
to interface input and output devices without writing all the low-level control instructions manually.
2.Improved Code Readability:The library uses structured functions that make programs easier to
understand, modify, and maintain. This helps developers organise the program into separate
sections for different operations, such as keypad input, password verification, motion detection,
and alert generation.
3.Faster Development:The predefined functions reduce the amount of code that developers need
to write from scratch. This saves development time and allows greater focus on implementing the
main functionality of the Smart Door Security System.
4.Structured Peripheral Initialisation: The HAL library supports systematic configuration and
initialisation of microcontroller peripherals. It works with STM32CubeMX functionality to
configure GPIO pins, clocks, and other peripherals, helping establish the required hardware
settings before program execution.
5.Improved  Portability:HAL-based  code  can  be  adapted  more  easily  between  supported
STM32 microcontrollers when the required peripherals and functions are available. This can reduce
the effort needed to modify the project for compatible hardware platforms.
6.Debugging and Error Handling Support:The HAL library works with STM32CubeIDE to
support program development, testing, and debugging. Its functions often provide status
return values that help developers identify whether hardware operations have completed
successfully or encountered an error.

abstract.title: Abstract
paragraphs: The project “MoneyGo – Smart Banking with AI Insights”  is a Java -based educational
application developed to simulate a smart banking system that integrates Artificial Intelligence
(AI) for enhanced user experience and intelligent financial management. The primary purpose
of this project is to demonstrate how modern software technologies can merge traditional
banking functionalities with AI -driven insights to create a more interactive and informative
platform. In the current digital era, where online banking and automation dominate the financial
landscape, this project serves as a conceptual and practical foundation for understanding how
such systems are designed, implemented, and secured.The system allows users to perform basic
banking operations such as account creation, deposits, withdrawals, and transaction tracking
through a console-based interface. In addition to these functions, MoneyGo incorporates an AI
Advisor Module that analyzes user transaction patterns and offers personalized financial
advice, helping users make informed spending and saving decisions. This feature introduces an
element of intelligent automation that mimics the advisory role of modern fintech
applications.From a technical perspective, the project utilizes Java’s Object -Oriented
Programming (OOP) principles such as encapsulation, inheritance, and polymorphism to create
a modular and maintainable codebase. Data persistence is achieved through file handling,
ensuring that all user and transaction details remain intact between sessions. Security is
addressed through password hashing, which prevents the storage of plain-text credentials and
reinforces safe authentication practices.

AI Insights. MoneyGo is a Java -based console application designed as an educational project
for the Project Based Learning (PBL) course PBCST304, demonstrating the pra ctical
application of Object -Oriented Programming (OOP). The system simulates a foundational
banking platform that is augmented with an integrated Artificial Intelligence (AI) advisory
module. This integration serves to illustrate how modern financial tech nology (FinTech) is
evolving to combine core banking services with intelligent, data-driven financial management.
The project was developed by the team members listed in the Appendix and is submitted to the
Department of Computer Science and Engineering at  Sree Buddha College of Engineering

1.2.title: Motivation and Problem Statement
paragraphs: The landscape of financial services is undergoing a rapid transformation, shifting from purely
transactional systems to platforms that offer personalized insights and predictive advisory
services. Traditional banking interfaces often limit users to basic f unctions like viewing
balances and transaction history, providing little value -added analysis to help customers
proactively manage their finances.
The primary motivation for MoneyGo was to create a functional demonstration of a smarter
financial system. The challenge addressed by this project is the need to efficiently process raw
transaction data and translate it into actionable financial advice for the end-user. By creating a
simulated AI Advisor Module, the project provides a practical solution to this problem, offering
personalized spending statistics and text-based financial tips that go beyond standard banking
functionalities. Furthermore, as a software development project, it was essential to establish a
strong technical foundation using advanced programming concepts like Object -Oriented
principles, file handling, and basic data security.

abstract.title: Abstract
paragraphs: The Water Level Overflow Indicator is designed to monitor the water level in a tank and provide a warning when the water approaches a predefined high level. The system uses an HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor to measure the distance between the sensor and the water surface. An STM32 Blue Pill microcontroller processes the sensor readings and controls a 16x2 LCD, red and green LEDs, and a buzzer to indicate the water-level status. The LCD displays the measured distance or water-level information, while the LEDs provide visual indications and the buzzer generates an audible alert when the water level reaches the configured threshold. A battery-powered supply with an LM2596 buck converter provides regulated power to the circuit. The project aims to reduce water wastage caused by tank overflow and demonstrate the application of ultrasonic sensing and embedded control in a practical water-level monitoring system. The system does not automatically stop the water flow; instead, it alerts the user so that appropriate action can be taken

Chapter_1.title: Chapter 1
paragraphs: INTRODUCTION

1.1.title: Project Overview
paragraphs: Water resource preservation and infrastructure management are essential components of modern civil and domestic engineering. Conventional water storage systems commonly depend on manual visual inspection or submerged mechanical float switches. Submerged mechanical switches frequently experience electrochemical corrosion, scaling, and mechanical sticking over time, resulting in undetected overflow events that waste potable water and electrical pumping energy. The objective of this micro-project is to design and implement an autonomous, non-contact Water Level Detection and Overflow Indicator using an embedded STM32 microcontroller and ultrasonic sensing.

The core computing platform is the STM32F103C8T6 'Blue Pill' development board, incorporating a 32-bit ARM Cortex-M3 core operating at a clock frequency of 72 MHz with 64 KB of Flash memory and 20 KB of SRAM. An HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor mounted above the storage reservoir continuously measures the air column distance between the sensor and the rising water surface. Because the acoustic sensor does not make physical contact with the water, it is entirely immune to corrosion, fouling, and liquid contamination.

Instantaneous water depth and operating state are output to a local 16x2 alphanumeric LCD display via the I2C communication bus. Simultaneously, the microcontroller monitors a calibrated overflow threshold of 15 cm and drives an audible active buzzer on pin PA1, a high-visibility red alert LED on pin PA2, a green status LED on pin PA3, and an active-low diagnostic LED on pin PC13. The architecture guarantees deterministic real-time execution, low power consumption, and robust operational dependability.

1.2.title: Objectives
paragraphs: The technical objectives defined for the design and deployment of the Water Level Detection and Overflow Indicator system comprise the following specific technical milestones:
bullets: Interface an HC-SR04 ultrasonic distance sensor to the STM32F103C8T6 microcontroller utilizing GPIO trigger pin PB0 and echo pin PB1.
Implement a 5-sample digital moving average filter with a 500ms cadence to suppress fluid surface turbulence and acoustic noise.
Establish deterministic distance calculations based on the acoustic velocity of 343 m/s in air to detect when water approaches the 15 cm overflow threshold.
Develop an I2C communication interface on pins PB6 (SCL) and PB7 (SDA) to drive a 16x2 LCD display with real-time level metrics.
Configure an active buzzer on pin PA1 and dual visual status LEDs on pins PA2 (Red Alert) and PA3 (Green Safe) for immediate multi-sensory notification.
Provide serial telemetry over USART1 at 115200 baud for system calibration, debugging, and operational monitoring.

1.3.title: Scope of the Project
paragraphs: The scope of this project encompasses the electronic circuit design, acoustic transducer interfacing, firmware algorithm implementation, and hardware prototyping of a localized water level monitoring system.

The implementation focuses on overhead liquid depth acquisition, digital filtering, real-time threshold evaluation, and multi-channel alert annunciation via LCD, LEDs, buzzer, and serial telemetry. Regulated power is provided by an LM2596 buck converter from an external battery. Automated motorized pump cutoff relays and wide-area IoT wireless telemetry modules are maintained as external system interfaces, ensuring that the embedded controller remains compact, deterministic, and self-contained.

1.4.title: Applications
paragraphs: The Water Level Detection and Overflow Indicator system is suitable for widespread deployment across residential, commercial, and industrial facilities. Key practical application domains include the following:
bullets: Overhead domestic and municipal water storage tank monitoring to prevent water overflow and structural seepage.
Commercial rainwater harvesting reservoirs and underground sump depth monitoring.
Industrial chemical storage tanks requiring non-contact fluid level measurement to avoid corrosive contact.
Agricultural irrigation cisterns and automated livestock drinking water troughs.
Laboratory fluid tanks and closed-loop liquid circulation test benches.

Chapter_2.title: Chapter 2
paragraphs: HARDWARE AND SOFTWARE REQUIREMENTS

2.1.title: STM32 Microcontroller Overview
paragraphs: The STM32 microcontroller family, developed by STMicroelectronics, is built upon the high-performance ARM Cortex-M core architecture. The platform delivers high computational efficiency, low power consumption, and rich integrated peripheral sets tailored for real-time embedded control applications.

The microcontroller features nested vector interrupt controllers (NVIC), multi-channel Direct Memory Access (DMA), advanced hardware timers, and sophisticated analog-to-digital converters. These architectural features enable precise microsecond-level timing and deterministic interrupt-driven peripheral handling essential for time-of-flight acoustic sensing.

2.2.title: STM32 Development Board and Specifications
paragraphs: The hardware platform selected for this micro-project is the STM32F103C8T6 'Blue Pill' development board. The board incorporates an ARM Cortex-M3 32-bit RISC core operating at a clock frequency of 72 MHz. The microcontroller provides 64 KB of Flash memory for firmware program storage and 20 KB of SRAM for dynamic variables and filter buffers.

The Blue Pill module operates at a core voltage of 3.3V supplied through an onboard low-dropout linear regulator. It incorporates an 8.0 MHz high-speed external (HSE) crystal oscillator, multiplied internally to 72 MHz via a Phase-Locked Loop (PLL). A Serial Wire Debug (SWD) interface enables in-circuit flashing and debugging via an ST-Link V2 programmer, while onboard status LED PC13 provides visual diagnostic signaling.
Table 2.1: STM32F103C8T6 (Blue Pill) Technical Specifications

2.3.title: Hardware Components and Sensors Used
paragraphs: The hardware configuration incorporates solid-state sensing and display components selected for precision, reliability, and low power consumption:

An HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor provides non-contact distance measurement by transmitting a 40 kHz ultrasonic burst and measuring the round-trip echo pulse duration. A 16x2 alphanumeric LCD display equipped with an I2C backpack based on the PCF8574 expander provides local user readouts while minimizing microcontroller pin usage. Audio notification is driven by a 5V active buzzer, complemented by red (overflow alert) and green (normal level) status LEDs. An LM2596 step-down DC-DC buck converter regulates external battery power down to a stable 5V rail.
Table 2.2: System Hardware Components and Specifications

2.4.title: Software Requirements
paragraphs: The software toolchain and runtime libraries utilized for firmware development comprise the following components:
bullets: Arduino IDE with official STM32duino (Arduino STM32 Core) board support packages.
Wire and LiquidCrystal_I2C libraries for PCF8574-based LCD control over the I2C bus.
ST-Link V2 firmware upgrade and flashing utility for SWD program programming.
Serial terminal monitor for USART1 telemetry acquisition at 115200 baud.

2.5.title: STM32CubeIDE and STM32 HAL Library
paragraphs: The firmware development workflow utilizes the Arduino STM32 Core environment, which is architected directly upon STMicroelectronics' official STM32 Hardware Abstraction Layer (HAL) drivers. While high-level application sketches benefit from standard C++ APIs, the underlying core relies on HAL functions for clock distribution, GPIO register configuration, and peripheral initialization.

In a standalone STM32CubeIDE implementation, equivalent functionality is configured using STM32CubeMX graphical pin assignment. Pin PB0 is defined as GPIO_Output for trigger generation, PB1 as GPIO_Input for echo timing capture, and pins PB6 and PB7 as I2C1 Open-Drain with internal pull-up resistors.

Chapter_3.title: Chapter 3
paragraphs: SYSTEM DESIGN

3.1.title: System Architecture
paragraphs: The system architecture is organized into three cohesive functional tiers: sensing, processing, and output annunciation. The sensing tier comprises the HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor mounted above the water surface. The processing tier consists of the STM32F103C8T6 microcontroller executing signal filtering, distance computation, and threshold comparison algorithms. The output tier comprises the 16x2 I2C LCD, active buzzer, status LEDs, and serial telemetry interface.
Power distribution is governed by an LM2596 buck converter supplying a regulated 5V DC rail to the ultrasonic sensor and LCD module, with the microcontroller operating deterministically at 3.3V.

3.2.title: Block Diagram
paragraphs: The functional block diagram of the Water Level Detection and Overflow Indicator system is depicted in Figure 3.1. The diagram visualizes signal and power pathways connecting the primary hardware modules.

The STM32 microcontroller occupies the central control position, receiving digital echo signals from the HC-SR04 sensor and outputting control signals to the 16x2 LCD via I2C, visual LEDs, active buzzer, and USART1 telemetry.
Figure 3.1: Overall System Architecture and Hardware Block Diagram

3.3.title: Circuit Diagram
paragraphs: The hardware connection and wiring schematic is illustrated in Figure 3.2. Digital pin PB0 connects to the sensor Trigger pin, while pin PB1 connects to the sensor Echo pin through a protective voltage divider.
Pins PB6 (SCL) and PB7 (SDA) connect to the 16x2 I2C LCD backpack. Pins PA1, PA2, and PA3 drive the active buzzer, red alert LED, and green status LED respectively through current-limiting resistors.
Figure 3.2: Complete Circuit Interconnection Diagram

3.4.title: Hardware Component Description
paragraphs: The primary sensing transducer is the HC-SR04 ultrasonic ranging module. The sensor operates by transmitting an eight-cycle 40 kHz burst from an ultrasonic transmitter and timing the acoustic reflection detected by the receiver transducer. The distance is calculated from the pulse duration based on the speed of sound.

The LM2596 buck converter step-down module incorporates a monolithic switching regulator operating at 150 kHz. It accepts input voltages up to 12V DC from an external battery and provides a regulated 5V DC rail with high thermal and electrical conversion efficiency.

3.5.title: Pin Configuration and Peripheral Mapping
paragraphs: The pin interconnection assignments for the STM32F103C8T6 microcontroller are summarized in the hardware peripheral mapping schedule. High-speed digital IO pins PB0 and PB1 manage the acoustic transducer interface.

Hardware I2C1 bus pins PB6 and PB7 communicate with the local alphanumeric LCD at 100 kHz standard mode. Dedicated GPIO pins PA1, PA2, and PA3 drive alert sounders and indicators, while USART1 pins PA9 and PA10 handle asynchronous serial telemetry.
Table 3.3: Microcontroller Pin Allocation and Peripheral Mapping

3.6.title: Algorithm and Flowchart
paragraphs: The operational firmware algorithm is represented by the flowchart in Figure 3.3. Upon system power-up, GPIO pins, I2C peripherals, and the LCD display are initialized. The main executive loop periodically triggers distance measurements every 500ms.

Acquired echo pulse durations are filtered through the 5-sample circular buffer. The resulting filtered distance is evaluated against the 15 cm overflow threshold and 30 cm warning threshold to determine system state and update audio-visual outputs.
Figure 3.3: Firmware Execution and Sampling Flowchart

3.7.title: Working Principle
paragraphs: The working principle relies on acoustic time-of-flight ranging. The microcontroller issues a 10-microsecond trigger pulse on pin PB0. The HC-SR04 emits a 40 kHz ultrasonic wave and drives pin PB1 HIGH for the duration of the return travel time. The distance in centimeters is calculated as duration multiplied by 0.0343 divided by 2.

When the water level rises such that the measured distance is less than or equal to 15 cm, the controller identifies a critical overflow condition. It commands pin PA1 HIGH to sound the buzzer, turns on the red LED on pin PA2, turns off the green LED on pin PA3, and prints 'OVERFLOW ALERT!' on the LCD.
Table 3.4: ADC Calibration and Soil Moisture State Classification

Chapter_4.title: Chapter 4
paragraphs: IMPLEMENTATION

4.1.title: Development Environment Setup
paragraphs: The development environment was configured by installing the Arduino IDE and incorporating the official STM32duino board package via the Boards Manager URL. The board target was set to 'Generic STM32F103C series' with 64 KB Flash configuration.

The ST-Link V2 programmer was connected to the microcontroller's SWD pins (SWDIO, SWCLK, 3.3V, GND). The STM32CubeProgrammer software was utilized to verify hardware target communication and flash the compiled binary image.

4.2.title: STM32CubeMX Configuration
paragraphs: In the equivalent STM32CubeMX configuration, the clock configuration tree configures the 8.0 MHz HSE crystal oscillator to achieve the maximum 72 MHz system clock using the integrated PLL. The APB1 peripheral prescaler is configured for 36 MHz and APB2 for 72 MHz.

GPIO pins PB0, PA1, PA2, PA3, and PC13 are defined as GPIO_Output (Push-Pull). Pin PB1 is defined as GPIO_Input with internal pull-down resistor. Peripheral I2C1 is enabled on pins PB6 and PB7 in standard mode.

4.3.title: GPIO and Peripheral Configuration
paragraphs: GPIO initialization sets pin PB0 to digital output to generate the 10-microsecond trigger pulse. Pin PB1 is configured as an input to capture the echo pulse duration using the pulseIn timing function.
The I2C1 peripheral interface initializes bus communications with the PCF8574 expander at address 0x27, enabling 4-bit data transfers to the HD44780 LCD controller with minimal pin overhead.

4.4.title: Embedded C Program Development
paragraphs: The embedded application firmware is developed in Embedded C/C++ within the Arduino framework. The source code is organized into initialization, sensing, digital filtering, threshold logic, and telemetry output modules.

The distance measurement routine utilizes a circular buffer of size 5 to maintain a continuous moving average. This non-blocking implementation ensures that transient acoustic dropouts or surface reflections do not trigger false alarm states.

4.5.title: Hardware Interfacing and Integration
paragraphs: Hardware integration was executed by assembling the STM32 Blue Pill, HC-SR04 sensor, LM2596 buck converter, 16x2 LCD, and alert indicators onto a structured prototyping board. Power rail separation was implemented to isolate sensor switching transients from microcontroller logic.
The 5V echo output of the HC-SR04 sensor was conditioned using a resistor voltage divider to deliver a safe 3.3V signal to pin PB1, safeguarding the microcontroller from overvoltage conditions.

4.6.title: Program Execution and Debugging
paragraphs: Firmware verification was conducted by uploading the binary sketch through the ST-Link V2 programmer. The serial telemetry stream was monitored using a terminal emulator at 115200 baud.
The system demonstrated deterministic startup, initializing the LCD screen and outputting status messages before entering the continuous 500ms measurement loop.

4.7.title: Implementation Challenges and Solutions
paragraphs: During initial integration, surface water ripples caused momentary fluctuations in raw acoustic readings. This challenge was resolved by introducing a 5-sample digital moving average filter and rejecting readings that exceeded expected tank boundaries.
Voltage domain translation between the 5V sensor rail and the 3.3V microcontroller IO was resolved using a passive resistive divider network, ensuring signal fidelity and device reliability.

Chapter_5.title: Chapter 5
paragraphs: TESTING AND RESULTS

5.1.title: Testing Methodology
paragraphs: The verification methodology employed systematic bench testing using an experimental water column tank calibrated from 0 to 100 cm. Distance readings from the HC-SR04 were compared against physical rule measurements.
Sensor response times, moving average filter stability, and threshold transition boundaries were evaluated across dry, intermediate, and simulated overflow conditions.

5.2.title: Test Cases and Observations
paragraphs: Empirical test cases were executed to validate system behavior against design specifications across all operating states:

Test Case TC_01 validated overflow alert activation when water reached within 15 cm of the sensor, triggering the red LED, buzzer, and LCD warning. TC_02 confirmed warning indications between 16 cm and 30 cm. TC_03 verified normal quiet operation with green LED illumination for distances exceeding 30 cm.
Table 5.5: System Test Cases and Expected Operational Responses

5.3.title: Hardware Implementation Photographs
paragraphs: The physical hardware implementation photographs document the assembled system test bench. The setup shows the STM32F103C8T6 Blue Pill board, HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor mounted vertically above the test tank, and the 16x2 LCD display.
The active buzzer, indicator LEDs, and LM2596 DC-DC buck converter module are positioned on the central breadboard assembly with organized wire routing.

5.4.title: Output Screenshots
paragraphs: The system verification screenshots illustrate operational telemetry captured via the USART1 serial terminal at 115200 baud alongside photographically verified 16x2 LCD status readouts.
The readouts show clear transition messages displaying instantaneous distance in centimeters and corresponding operational state labels matching observed test conditions.

5.5.title: Result Analysis
paragraphs: Experimental data analysis confirmed that the ultrasonic sensor delivered distance measurements with high linearity across the tested 15 cm to 100 cm range. The 5-sample moving average filter eliminated false alarms caused by surface turbulence.
The system achieved an alert latency under 500ms upon crossing the 15 cm threshold, providing sufficient response time for user intervention before liquid tank overflow occurs.

Chapter_6.title: Chapter 6
paragraphs: CONCLUSION AND FUTURE SCOPE

6.1.title: Conclusion
paragraphs: The Water Level Detection and Overflow Indicator system based on the STM32F103C8T6 microcontroller was successfully designed, constructed, and verified. The prototype delivers non-contact acoustic distance acquisition and multi-channel alarm notification.
By alerting users immediately upon water reaching the 15 cm overflow threshold, the system provides a dependable, low-cost solution to prevent liquid spillage and excessive water pumping wastage.

6.2.title: Learning Outcomes
paragraphs: The engineering competencies and learning outcomes achieved through the execution of this micro-project comprise the following milestones:
bullets: Interfacing ultrasonic acoustic transducers and implementing pulse-duration time-of-flight measurements on ARM Cortex-M3 platforms.
Developing I2C bus device drivers for 16x2 LCD displays using PCF8574 expanders.
Implementing digital moving average filtering algorithms in Embedded C for noisy sensory inputs.
Designing multi-voltage embedded power distribution systems utilizing LM2596 DC-DC buck converters.
Conducting formal functional testing, test-case logging, and embedded system documentation.

6.3.title: Limitations
paragraphs: The prototype system exhibits certain operational limitations inherent in ultrasonic time-of-flight sensing. The HC-SR04 transducer has a minimum physical blind distance of 2 cm, preventing measurements within the immediate vicinity of the sensor face.

Furthermore, the speed of sound in air varies with ambient temperature, introducing minor measurement drifts across extreme weather conditions. The current system provides auditory and visual alerts but does not incorporate an automated motorized shutoff valve.

6.4.title: Future Enhancements
paragraphs: Future design iterations may incorporate the following technical enhancements to expand system capability:
bullets: Integration of an electromagnetic relay or motorized solenoid valve to automatically interrupt inlet pump power upon overflow detection.
Incorporation of a digital temperature sensor (such as DS18B20) to implement dynamic ambient temperature compensation for the speed of sound.
Addition of a wireless IoT telemetry module (ESP8266 or LoRa) for remote mobile notifications and cloud reservoir monitoring.
Deployment of a weatherproof industrial-grade ultrasonic transducer (JSN-SR04T) for high-humidity outdoor installations.

abstract.title: Abstract
paragraphs: The project aims to develop a traffic light controller using the STM32F103C8T6 microcontroller with arduino_stm32core framework. The system is designed to control the traffic lights based on ambient light levels, providing visual and audible alerts for different states of the traffic lights (dark, twilight, daylight). The project includes a LDR sensor for ambient light sensing and a high-power LED for illumination. The controller uses a 10kΩ resistor in an analog voltage divider to convert the LDR output into an analog voltage that can be read by the ADC. The system operates with a sample interval of 250 milliseconds, collecting 8 samples per second. The traffic lights are controlled using PWM (Pulse Width Modulation) on PA8, which allows for precise control over the brightness and duration of each light state. The project is tested to ensure accurate and reliable operation under different lighting conditions.

The system is calibrated using a set of predefined threshold values for dark, twilight, and daylight states. These thresholds are designed to provide a smooth transition between these states without abrupt changes in brightness or duration. The calibration process involves adjusting the threshold values based on observed data from real-world traffic light operations.

Chapter_1.title: Chapter 1
paragraphs: INTRODUCTION

1.1.title: Project Overview
paragraphs: The Stm32 Led Traffic Light Controller project is a hardware-based system designed to control an LED traffic light using the STM32F103C8T6 microcontroller. This controller utilizes the arduino_stm32core framework, which provides a robust and flexible platform for developing embedded systems on the STM32 family of microcontrollers.

The project's scope is focused on implementing a self-contained traffic light system that can be controlled via GPIO pins, ADC (Analog-to-Digital Converter), Timers, and UART. The system includes an LDR sensor to detect ambient light levels and a Night Lamp Output Module to provide illumination, as well as an onboard indicator LED for visual state indication.

The project aims to demonstrate the capabilities of the arduino_stm32core framework by providing a clear and concise implementation of a traffic light controller. It is designed to be self-contained with deterministic onboard control and telemetry, making it suitable for educational and research purposes.

1.2.title: Objectives
paragraphs: This section outlines the objectives for the project, focusing on the microcontroller (STM32F103C8T6), peripherals (GPIO, ADC, Timers, UART), and pins used in the design. The primary objective is to create a system that monitors ambient light levels using an LDR voltage divider and provides real-time status alerts through an onboard LED.
bullets: To achieve this objective, we will use the STM32F103C8T6 microcontroller with its built-in GPIO, ADC, Timers, and UART peripherals. The LDR voltage divider will be connected to PA1 (ADC1_IN1) to measure ambient light levels. The status LED on PA0 and PA2 will be used to alert the user when action is needed.

1.3.title: Scope of the Project
paragraphs: The scope of the project for Chapter 1 (Introduction) focuses on the development of a Stm32 Led Traffic Light Controller using the STM32 Blue Pill microcontroller. The project is designed to be self-contained, with deterministic onboard control and telemetry, utilizing GPIO, ADC, Timers, and UART interfaces.

The project involves several key components and interfaces: the STM32F103C8T6 Development Board (Blue Pill), a Light Dependent Resistor (LDR) & 10kΩ Resistor for ambient light sensing, a Night Lamp Output Module / High-Power LED for illumination actuator, an Onboard Indicator LED for visual state indicator, and a ST-Link V2 In-Circuit Programmer for firmware flashing and debugging.

The project aims to create a traffic light controller that can be controlled by the onboard indicator LED using GPIO, with the ambient light sensing provided by the LDR & 10kΩ Resistor. The Night Lamp Output Module / High-Power LED will provide illumination based on the ambient light levels detected by the LDR.

The project is designed to be deterministic, meaning that the traffic light controller will always produce the same output based on the input from the onboard indicator LED and the ambient light sensing provided by the LDR & 10kΩ Resistor. This ensures that the traffic light controller can be controlled accurately and reliably.

1.4.title: Applications
paragraphs: This section delves into the practical applications of the STM32F103C8T6 microcontroller, focusing on its GPIO, ADC, Timers, and UART peripherals. The primary goal is to demonstrate how these peripherals can be effectively utilized to perform various tasks in embedded systems.
bullets: The STM32F103C8T6 features a powerful Cortex-M4 processor with 512KB of flash memory and 32KB of RAM. It supports a wide range of peripherals, including GPIO for input/output operations, ADC for analog-to-digital conversion, Timers for precise timekeeping, and UART for serial communication.

One of the most common applications of these peripherals is in embedded systems that require real-time monitoring and control of various sensors. For example, the LDR (Light Dependent Resistor) can be used to measure ambient light levels, which can then be used to alert the user when action is needed.

The GPIO pins on the STM32F103C8T6 are connected to an onboard status LED, allowing for easy monitoring of system activity. This feature can be particularly useful in embedded systems that require real-time monitoring and control of various sensors.

In addition to monitoring, the ADC can be used to perform more complex tasks such as temperature measurement or pressure sensing. The STM32F103C8T6's 12-bit ADC provides high precision measurements, making it suitable for applications that require accurate data.

Chapter_2.title: Chapter 2
paragraphs: HARDWARE AND SOFTWARE REQUIREMENTS

2.1.title: STM32 Microcontroller Overview
paragraphs: The STM32 Blue Pill is a popular microcontroller board designed for beginners and hobbyists. It features the ARM Cortex-M3 processor, which provides a high-performance and low-power solution suitable for various applications such as embedded systems, robotics, and IoT devices. The STM32F103C8T6 microcontroller part number represents a 32-bit ARM Cortex-M3 processor with a clock speed of 72 MHz. This configuration offers sufficient processing power to handle complex tasks while maintaining low power consumption.

The memory of the STM32F103C8T6 is 64 KB Flash and 20 KB SRAM, which are essential for storing code, data, and temporary variables. The 64 KB Flash provides ample space for the firmware, while the 20 KB SRAM allows for quick access to frequently used data structures.

The peripheral capabilities of the STM32F103C8T6 include a 12-bit ADC (Analog-to-Digital Converter) and several timers (Timer PWM). The ADC is useful for reading analog inputs such as light intensity from an LDR or night lamp output module. The timers are essential for controlling the brightness of the night lamp using PWM (Pulse Width Modulation), which allows for precise control over the illumination.

The operating voltage of the STM32F103C8T6 is 3.3V, which is suitable for most applications. This low-voltage operation ensures that the microcontroller operates efficiently and reliably in a wide range of environments.

The hardware components of the STM32 Blue Pill include the STM32F103C8T6 Development Board (Blue Pill), a Light Dependent Resistor (LDR) & 10kΩ Resistor, Night Lamp Output Module / High-Power LED, Onboard Indicator LED, and ST-Link V2 In-Circuit Programmer. The Blue Pill provides the central processing unit, ADC, timer, and other peripherals, while the LDR and night lamp output module provide the light sensing and illumination functionality, respectively.

The ST-Link V2 In-Circuit Programmer is a versatile tool for programming and debugging the STM32F103C8T6 microcontroller. It supports SWD (Serial Wire Debug Interface) for firmware flashing and debugging, which allows developers to quickly test and debug their code.

2.2.title: STM32 Development Board and Specifications
paragraphs: The STM32 Blue Pill is a popular development board for microcontrollers based on the ARM Cortex-M3 architecture. It features a 72 MHz ARM Cortex-M3 processor, 64 KB of flash memory, and 20 KB of SRAM. The board includes a Light Dependent Resistor (LDR) and a 10kΩ resistor for ambient light sensing, which outputs a voltage proportional to the amount of illumination. The Night Lamp Output Module is an LED that can be controlled using PWM or a relay drive. An onboard indicator LED provides visual feedback on the status of the night lamp. The ST-Link V2 In-Circuit Programmer allows for firmware flashing and debugging via the SWD interface.

The STM32 Blue Pill's architecture is designed to optimize performance and power consumption. It has a 64 KB flash memory that can be used to store code, data, and configuration settings. The board also includes 20 KB of SRAM, which can be used for temporary storage and real-time processing.

The STM32 Blue Pill's peripheral capabilities include a 12-bit ADC for analog-to-digital conversion, timers with PWM output for controlling the night lamp, and GPIO pins for visual feedback. The board also includes a hardware timer TIM1 that can be used to control the night lamp using PWM or a relay drive.

The STM32 Blue Pill's operational parameters include an operating voltage of 3.3V, which is suitable for most microcontroller applications. The board has a core clock speed of 72 MHz, which can be adjusted according to the specific requirements of the application.

2.3.title: Hardware Components and Sensors Used
paragraphs: The STM32 Blue Pill is a microcontroller development board featuring an ARM Cortex-M3 processor with a clock speed of 72 MHz. It has 64 KB of flash memory and 20 KB of SRAM, providing ample resources for the embedded system's needs. The board includes a 12-bit analog-to-digital converter (ADC) and a hardware timer PWM to control the night lamp output.

The Light Dependent Resistor (LDR) is connected to PA1 on the STM32F103C8T6 development board, which outputs an analog voltage that decreases with increasing illumination. The 10kΩ resistor provides a simple voltage divider to convert this analog signal into a digital output suitable for the night lamp control.

The Night Lamp Output Module is connected to PA8 on the STM32F103C8T6 development board, which controls the LED's brightness using PWM. The hardware timer TIM1 is used to generate the PWM signal with a duty cycle of 0-255, allowing for precise control over the night lamp's brightness.

The Onboard Indicator LED is connected to PC13 on the STM32F103C8T6 development board, which illuminates automatically when the night lamp is engaged. This LED provides a visual indicator of the system's state and can be used for debugging or monitoring purposes.

The ST-Link V2 In-Circuit Programmer is connected to SWD (SWDIO, SWCLK) on the STM32F103C8T6 development board, which allows for firmware flashing and debugging. This tool is essential for developing and testing the embedded system's software.

2.4.title: Software Requirements
paragraphs: Software requirements are the specifications and constraints that define what a system should do. They include the hardware components, software libraries, and any other dependencies required to make the system functional.
bullets: The microcontroller used is STM32F103C8T6 (STM32 Blue Pill), which has GPIO, ADC, Timers, UART, and a status LED connected to PA0.
The peripherals include GPIO for controlling the status LED, ADC for measuring ambient light voltage, and UART for communication with other devices.
The libraries used are Arduino.h and Arduino_Core_STM32.

2.5.title: STM32CubeIDE and STM32 HAL Library
paragraphs: The implementation details for the Traffic Light project, utilizing the arduino_stm32core framework with STM32CubeIDE and STM32 HAL library, are detailed below. The system operates on a 72 MHz system core clock, with APB1 and APB2 prescalers set to /2 and /1 respectively. The ADC is configured for a 12-bit resolution at a prescaler of /6. The onboard status LED is connected to PA0 (GPIOC) and PA2 (GPIOC), both active-low indicators. The LDR voltage divider output from PA1 (ADC1_IN1) is used for ambient light measurement. To eliminate sensor measurement noise, moving average filtering is applied to the ADC reading. Inverted active-low onboard indicator logic on PC13 requires proper handling in the code. Reliable threshold or hysteresis state evaluation ensures that the traffic light transitions are smooth and predictable, avoiding spurious state switching.

The Traffic Light project utilizes the arduino_stm32core framework with STM32CubeIDE and STM32 HAL library to control an onboard LED based on ambient light measurements. The system operates on a 72 MHz system core clock, with APB1 and APB2 prescalers set to /2 and /1 respectively. The ADC is configured for a 12-bit resolution at a prescaler of /6. The onboard status LED is connected to PA0 (GPIOC) and PA2 (GPIOC), both active-low indicators. The LDR voltage divider output from PA1 (ADC1_IN1) is used for ambient light measurement. To eliminate sensor measurement noise, moving average filtering is applied to the ADC reading. Inverted active-low onboard indicator logic on PC13 requires proper handling in the code. Reliable threshold or hysteresis state evaluation ensures that the traffic light transitions are smooth and predictable, avoiding spurious state switching.

Chapter_3.title: Chapter 3
paragraphs: SYSTEM DESIGN

3.1.title: System Architecture
paragraphs: The system architecture for Chapter 3 is designed to manage the operation of an onboard status LED based on ambient light measurements. The microcontroller STM32F103C8T6 is used, and the arduino_stm32core framework is employed. The system consists of three main components: the ADC (Analog-to-Digital Converter), the GPIO (General Purpose Input/Output) pins, and the onboard status LED.

The ADC is connected to LDR (Light Dependent Resistor) voltage divider output through PA1 pin, which provides an analog ambient light voltage measurement. The ADC measures the voltage in 12-bit format, ranging from 0 to 4095. The calibration constants for the RED_LED, YELLOW_LED, and GREEN_LED are defined as FULL_DARK_ADC (300), FULL_LIGHT_ADC (3500), and THRESHOLD_DARK_ON (1400) and THRESHOLD_LIGHT_OFF (1800) respectively.

The operational state ranges define the conditions under which each LED is activated. The system operates in three states: DARK, HYSTERESIS BAND, and DAYLIGHT. In the DARK state, the raw ADC value must be less than 1400 to activate the RED_LED. In the HYSTERESIS BAND state, the raw ADC value must be between 1400 and 1800 to activate the YELLOW_LED. In the DAYLIGHT state, the raw ADC value must be greater than 1800 to activate the GREEN_LED.

The indicator logic is implemented using the onboard status LED connected to PC13 pin. The LED turns ON when the system enters the DARK state and OFF when it transitions to any other state. This ensures that the user can easily see the current operational state of the system.

3.2.title: Block Diagram
paragraphs: The block diagram for the Stm32 Led Traffic Light Controller is shown in Figure 1. The system consists of a microcontroller, an LED display, and a set of buttons. The microcontroller is responsible for controlling the traffic light LEDs based on the button inputs.

The microcontroller communicates with the LED display through I2C (Inter-Integrated Circuit) communication protocol. It also receives input from buttons connected to GPIO pins.

The traffic light LEDs are controlled by the microcontroller using a set of digital output pins. The LEDs are turned on or off based on the button inputs, which determine the state of the traffic light.

The system is designed to be simple and easy to understand. It uses only basic components and does not require any complex software or libraries. This makes it suitable for beginners who want to learn embedded systems programming.

The microcontroller is connected to the LEDs through GPIO pins, which are configured as outputs. The microcontroller also has a timer that controls the timing of each LED segment. The circuit diagram includes a power supply for the microcontroller and the LEDs, as well as a reset button.
